opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say Jensen hasn't changed that much at his core, and I think that's actually the remarkable part.

When I joined in 2016, Nvidia was already doing well in deep learning, but it was still a much smaller company than it is today. Since then the market value and the attention around the company have grown enormously, and Jensen has become a kind of public figure far beyond the tech industry. But when you're in a meeting with him, he's still the same person. He's still extremely hands-on, he still asks very detailed technical questions, and he still wants to understand things from first principles. He doesn't just want the summary slide. He wants to know why something works, what the bottleneck is, and what it would take to make it ten times better.

One thing that has stayed constant is his intensity and his sense of urgency. Even when the company is doing great, he talks as if we're thirty days from going out of business. It sounds like a joke, but he really means it. That mindset keeps everyone humble and pushes us to keep moving.

If anything has changed, I'd say the scope of his vision has expanded. Back then, a lot of the conversation was about GPUs for training neural networks. Now he talks about AI factories, accelerated computing for every industry, robotics, and what he calls physical AI. For people like me working on generative models and world models, that's very exciting, because he's thinking very far ahead and he's willing to invest in directions before they're obvious to everyone else.

And he's still very approachable as a leader. He has a very flat organization, a lot of direct reports, and he likes information to flow openly. Researchers can present directly to him and get very direct feedback. Sometimes the feedback is tough, but it's always about making the work better. So for me, the consistency of who he is, combined with how much bigger his ambitions have become, is the most striking thing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the person himself hasn't changed that much. When I joined in 2016, Jensen was already Jensen — very intense, very direct, asking very sharp questions, and expecting you to know your stuff. That part is the same today. What's changed is the scale around him, and how he spends his attention.

In 2016, Nvidia was still mostly seen as a gaming company. Deep learning was happening, but it was a bet. I remember he would come to research talks, sit in the front, and ask detailed technical questions — about the architecture, about the data, why this result and not that one. He was very hands-on with the technical direction, and he knew who the researchers were and what they were working on. Back then it felt like a big startup, and he could touch almost everything.

Now the company is many times bigger, and AI is no longer a bet, it's the center of everything. So he has to operate at a different altitude. He thinks much more about the whole stack — chips, systems, networking, software, and also the ecosystem, the partners, the countries. He talks about "AI factories," about sovereign AI, about physical AI and robotics. His framing has become much larger. But what surprises people is that he still goes very deep. He will still send an email at midnight about a specific paper, or ask why a model in our group is behind on some benchmark. He reads a lot. He still knows the details, maybe not every one, but enough that you cannot hide behind a slide.

I think another change is that he has become more patient with long-horizon bets, and at the same time more urgent about execution. He says things like "the speed of light" — we should be limited only by physics, not by process. That urgency was always there, but now it comes with a very clear strategic picture of where things are going five, ten years out. For example, when I started working on generative models and simulation, the story we could tell was mostly about graphics and content. Now he connects that directly to robotics, to autonomous vehicles, to the next trillion-dollar opportunity. He saw that pattern earlier than most of us.

And the last thing — he's become much more of a public figure. In 2016 he was known in the industry; now he's known everywhere. But inside the company, in meetings, he's the same person: the leather jacket, the whiteboard, the tough questions, and also, honestly, a lot of care for people. He remembers things about you. So the external image changed a lot, the environment changed a lot, but the core, I'd say, is remarkably consistent.
